newsitem.title: USA: Defiant Key West celebrates Hemingway's life.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Key West celebrates Hemingway's life.

text.p: Defiant in the face of adversity, Key West is honouring its legendary former resident Ernest Hemingway with a fiesta in the streets and bars where the writer once caroused.
Men with white beards and hefty paunches have descended on this beachcomber's paradise at the tip of the Florida Keys to take their chances in the famous Hemingway look-alike contest.

The festival also features an arm-wrestling competition, literary events and a mock running of the bulls after the San Fermin festival in Pamplona, Spain, which Hemingway wrote about in "The Sun Also Rises."

This year's Hemingway Days Festival was taking place Thursday through Sunday despite a bruising battle with Hemingway's sons, who said the boozy Key West event dishonoured the late Nobel Laureate's legacy by portraying him as a slob and a bum.
To ease the affront, they demanded a share of the profits from festival organisers in return for their blessing. Organisers said in April the festival, which has run since 1981, was cancelled.

But after the Hemingway family announced an alternative celebration in Sanibel, an upscale resort on Florida's West Coast, Key West decided it was better to have than have not and to hold the festival after all.

"We're delighted to honour Hemingway again and we don't intend to have any less fun this year," festival director Carol Shaunghnessy told Reuters. "We've always presented a blend celebrating him as a literary icon as well as his lifestyle.

"Hemingway wrote very serious things but he always had a good time here. He is indelibly tied to Key West. His legacy is what began Key West's literary renaissance and the people and the lifestyle contributed to his writing," she said.
The Island News praised Key West's citizens for going ahead with the festival "despite threats and demands for money".
"We don't believe we 'own' Hemingway as some have said but we do own the right to celebrate the life of man who left his mark on our tiny island," it said in an editorial.

Hemingway lived in Key West from 1929 to 1940 and wrote such classics there as the bullfighting book "Death in the Afternoon" and "The Snows of Kilimanjaro"." The novel "To Have and Have Not" portrays Depression-era Key West.

He also fished in its waters and raised hell in its bars with a bunch of cronies that included Joe Russell, founder of Sloppy Joe's. In those days you could also hop on a ferry to Havana, Cuba, 90 miles (145 km) across the Florida Strait, for a shot of more exotic fun.
Hemingway met his third wife Martha Gelhorn in Key West, at the bar of the original Sloppy Joe's, now Captain Tony's Saloon. His former house on Whitehead Street is a big tourist attraction.

Amid the mano a mano over the festival, the Hemingway House's present owners bought the rights to the festival from Michael Walton and decided to fight Hemingway sons John, Patrick and Gregory, who are represented by Fashion Licensing of America.

The event last weekend in Sanibel, where Hemingway never set foot, was an altogether more sedate affair, with tennis and golf tournaments, and writing, poetry and photography contests and readings. Son Patrick Hemingway told reporters: "We don't really care about Key West and their festival -- that's their business."
Back at Sloppy Joe's on Duvall Street on Friday morning, look-alike Jim McGill from Hollywood, Florida, nursed a morning beer at the bar.
"Hemingway should be in the public domain," he said.

McGill, a retired journalist, said he had been taking part in Hemingway look alike contests since 1992. He had triumphed in Oak Park, Illinois, Hemingway's birthplace, but not yet at Key West. "The festival was simply a great way to have fun for a few days," he said.
"We have a few drinks, go out in a sailboat, swim. I'm not going to say we don't get drunk but we don't make trouble."
